description_ru: Текст о фазах сна, внутренних часах и о том, почему мозгу необходим ночной отдых для памяти и здоровья.
text:
For many centuries, sleep was thought to be a kind of switching off, a period when the brain simply rested while the body recovered. Modern research has shown that this idea was completely wrong. During the night, the brain is remarkably active, and some of its most important work is carried out when we are unconscious. Scientists now believe that sleep is as essential to human health as food and water, and that people who are deprived of it suffer in surprising ways.

A typical night is not one long block of unconscious rest. It is divided into cycles of about ninety minutes, and most adults go through four or five of them. Each cycle contains several stages. In the first, light sleep, the heartbeat slows down and the muscles relax, and it is easy to be woken by a small noise. People who are woken during this stage often insist that they were not asleep at all.

Next comes deeper sleep, in which the body temperature falls and the brain waves become larger and slower. The deepest stage, which is dominant in the first half of the night, is sometimes called slow-wave sleep. During this phase, the body releases growth hormone, repairs tissues and strengthens the immune system. It is also the hardest stage to wake up from, and anyone who has been disturbed in the middle of it may feel confused and heavy for several minutes.

The most famous stage is REM sleep, named after the rapid eye movements that occur beneath the eyelids. The brain becomes almost as active as it is during the day, the heart beats faster and vivid dreams take place. At the same time, the body is temporarily paralysed, so that people do not act out what they are dreaming. This is a clever safety mechanism, and when it fails, as it does in certain rare disorders, sleepers can be seen punching and kicking in their beds.

Why do we feel sleepy at all? Two main systems are responsible. The first is a chemical called adenosine, which builds up in the brain throughout the day and creates a growing pressure to sleep. Caffeine works by blocking the receptors that detect it, so it does not remove tiredness, but merely hides it for a while. The second system is the body clock, a tiny cluster of nerve cells that follows a rhythm of roughly twenty-four hours and is influenced mainly by light.

When darkness falls, the clock tells the brain to produce melatonin, a hormone that prepares the body for sleep. Bright light, especially the bluish light of phones and tablets, can delay this signal, so that people who use screens late at night find it harder to fall asleep. Teenagers are particularly affected, because their body clocks naturally shift later during adolescence. This is one reason why an early start at school is a constant struggle for many of them, and why some researchers have argued that lessons should begin later.

Sleep also plays a crucial role in memory. During the night, the brain replays the experiences of the day and decides which ones are worth keeping. Facts and skills that have been practised before bedtime are transferred into long-term storage, and in experiments, students who slept after studying remembered considerably more than those who stayed awake. Evidence from animal studies also suggests that during deep sleep, the brain flushes out waste products that accumulate while we are awake, although this research is still developing.

The consequences of poor sleep are serious. After a single bad night, people become irritable, react more slowly and find it difficult to concentrate. Over the long term, a chronic lack of sleep has been linked to heart disease, diabetes, weakened immunity and depression. Perhaps the most dangerous effect is that tired people are poor judges of their own condition. Studies have shown that drivers who have been awake for eighteen hours perform about as badly as those who have been drinking.

Most adults need between seven and nine hours of sleep, although individual needs vary, and the idea that some people can function perfectly on four hours is mostly a myth. A few simple habits can help. It is advisable to go to bed and wake up at the same time every day, to keep the bedroom cool and dark, and to avoid heavy meals and caffeine in the evening. Exercise during the day also improves sleep, as long as it is not done too close to bedtime.

Sleep, in short, is not a luxury or a waste of time. It is the period in which the body repairs itself and the mind sorts out its memories. The next time somebody tells you that they will sleep when they are dead, you might politely point out that, according to science, the plan is not likely to be a long one.

Скользите от «а» к «и»; звук должен быть долгим.
Выделяйте ударный слог (un-CON-scious, a-DEN-o-sine, ad-o-LES-cence), остальные слоги ослабляйте.

What happens to the body during REM sleep?
questions.answer: The brain is very active, dreams occur and the body is paralysed.

questions.question: What does caffeine do?
questions.answer: It blocks the receptors that detect adenosine, hiding tiredness.
